openingProblem.problem: In 1968 Moscow crushed a reform movement led by the Communist Party itself. In 1980 ten million Poles joined a union the party did not control. Was Soviet control stronger or weaker after 1968?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did 1968 strengthen or weaken Soviet control?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: The Prague Spring, 1968
chunks.body:
On 5 January 1968 the Czechoslovak Central Committee replaced the Stalinist Antonín Novotný with **Alexander Dubček**, a 47-year-old Slovak from the reform wing of the party. Dubček was a loyal Communist, but public rallies soon demanded an end to censorship and an inquiry into the purges of the 1950s, and he went with the tide. In the spring the Central Committee adopted an **Action Programme**: autonomy for Slovakia, rehabilitation of past victims and the "democratization" of the political and economic system. Over a ten-year transition, other parties would be allowed to compete in genuine elections. People called it "Socialism with a human face".

On 26 June censorship was formally abolished. The next day the writer Ludvík Vaculík published "Two Thousand Words", calling for political parties and citizens' committees to push reform further. Dubček rejected it. He would not give up the party's monopoly, which he saw as the only vehicle for safe change.

Tony Judt argues that the Prague Spring rested on three illusions. The first was that freedom could be folded into Communism. The second was that the party could allow free speech without losing control. The third and most dangerous was Dubček's belief that he could keep Moscow at bay. The reformers thought Imre Nagy's mistake in 1956 had been to leave the Warsaw Pact; so long as Czechoslovakia stayed in the alliance, they believed, Moscow would leave them alone. But "by 1968, the Soviet Union was worried less about military security than the Party's loss of monopoly control."

Moscow's fear was contagion. In March the Ukrainian leader Petro Shelest reported that news from Prague was affecting young Ukrainians; Polish and East German leaders complained. In April the Soviet defence minister was told to plan military operations. On 14 July the leaders of the USSR, Poland, East Germany, Bulgaria and Hungary sent Prague a warning letter. At Bratislava on 3 August Brezhnev set out the doctrine that would bear his name: each party was free to apply socialism in its own way, but not to deviate from its principles, because "the weakening of any of the links in the world system of socialism directly affects all the socialist countries". The same day five members of the Czechoslovak Praesidium secretly asked Moscow to intervene. This mattered because the Soviet leaders could now present an invasion as a response to an invitation, which meant that the decision of 18 August faced no serious obstacle.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Prague Spring threatened Moscow because it undermined the party's monopoly, not the alliance.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Dubček himself defended the monopoly and rejected 'Two Thousand Words'.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Contagion was the Soviet fear: neighbouring leaders demanded action.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Brezhnev seems to have been reluctant, so the decision was not automatic.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The abolition of censorship let pressure from below outrun the party.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Federalisation, a moderate reform, survived the invasion, so not every reform was unacceptable.

howItGetsAsked: Discuss the view that the Prague Spring failed because Dubček misjudged Moscow.
Analyse the reasons for the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Dubček's central mistake in 1968 was to misread the lesson of Hungary in 1956.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The reformers believed Nagy's error had been to leave the Warsaw Pact, so they stayed loyal to the alliance while abolishing censorship on 26 June.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant they reassured Moscow on the wrong point, since, as Judt argues, the Soviet leaders now feared the party's loss of monopoly control more than any military threat.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Dubček himself defended the party's monopoly and rejected Vaculík's call for new parties, so his own aims were limited.
useItInAnEssay.judge: His misjudgement was therefore not about his intentions but about how Moscow would read the freedom he allowed.

chunks.title: Invasion, normalisation and the Brezhnev Doctrine
chunks.body:
On **21 August 1968** some 500,000 troops from the USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany entered Czechoslovakia. Moscow knew there was no risk from the West: five weeks earlier Washington and Moscow had co-signed the Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty, and the United States was absorbed in Vietnam. The Czechoslovak government asked people not to resist with arms, and they did not, but there were street protests and passive resistance. The Soviet leaders, who had expected a welcome, were surprised.

Dubček and his colleagues were arrested, flown to Moscow and made to sign away parts of their programme. They were allowed back for a few months because they had public support, but **"normalization"** began at once: censorship returned and the planned party congress was cancelled. In January 1969 the student Jan Palach set fire to himself in Wenceslas Square in protest; his funeral became a day of national mourning. On 17 April 1969 Dubček was replaced by **Gustáv Husák**, a Slovak who had himself been imprisoned under Stalin and so could purge the reformers without looking like a Stalinist.

The repression was quieter than in the 1950s but thorough. There were no great public trials. Instead, people active in 1968 were asked to sign statements renouncing it. Those who refused lost their jobs, and their children suffered too. Poets and playwrights ended up cleaning boilers and washing windows. The regime offered the "carrot of consumer goods and the stick of omnipresent surveillance".

Judt sees 1968 as more decisive than 1956. The Kremlin had shown that socialist states had only limited sovereignty and that any lapse in the party's monopoly might bring tanks; after 1968, Soviet control was "firmly underwritten" by that knowledge. But the price was legitimacy. The illusion that Communism could be reformed "was crushed under the tanks on August 21st 1968 and it never recovered". Never again would reformers look to the ruling party to carry their hopes. This mattered because after 1968 the regimes rested on force and material bribery alone, which meant that, in Judt's phrase, Communism staggered on "sustained by an unlikely alliance of foreign loans and Russian bayonets".

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Brezhnev Doctrine secured Soviet control for two decades by making the threat of force credible.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It depended on Moscow's willingness to use force, which would vanish under Gorbachev.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Normalisation worked through humiliation and consumerism rather than terror.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The threat of violence was always implicit, so fear still underpinned it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: 1968 destroyed belief in reform Communism, so regimes lost their last claim to consent.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Kádár's Hungary still won a measure of acceptance through material concessions.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent did the Brezhnev Doctrine secure Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1968 and 1981?
Analyse the reasons for the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The invasion of 1968 secured Soviet control but destroyed the legitimacy of Communist rule.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 21 August 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops entered Czechoslovakia, and by April 1969 Husák had replaced Dubček and begun purging the reformers.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Moscow had proved it would use force against any lapse in the party's monopoly, so no satellite leader would risk reform for two decades.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt argues that the illusion that Communism could be reformed was crushed under the tanks and never recovered, so the regimes lost any claim to consent.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The invasion therefore strengthened control in the short term while hollowing out its foundations.

chunks.title: Kádár, Ceauşescu and the dissidents
chunks.body:
After 1968 the satellite regimes sought stability in different ways. Judt identifies three models. In **Hungary**, Kádár introduced the New Economic Mechanism in 1968: collective farms gained autonomy and were encouraged to support private plots, some prices followed the world market, and private shops were allowed. The aim was the most market activity compatible with "undiluted political control". Kádár offered Hungarians consumer goods and even access to the West as rewards for good behaviour; Hungary became "the best barracks in the laager". After 1968 every regime except Romania adopted his approach of asking only for outward conformity.

**Romania** took the road of "national Stalinism". Soviet troops had left in 1958. Under Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej and, from 1965, Nicolae Ceauşescu, Romania refused to allow Warsaw Pact manoeuvres on its soil, stayed out of Moscow's quarrel with China and cut its trade with Comecon from 70 to 45 per cent of the total. Ceauşescu declined even to attend the Bratislava meeting of August 1968. The West rewarded him: President Nixon visited Bucharest in August 1969, and Romania joined GATT, the IMF and the World Bank. But inside, Romanian Communism was "peculiarly vicious and repressive" and allowed no opposition at all. Independence from Moscow did not mean freedom.

Opposition took a new form. The **Helsinki Final Act** of August 1975 gave Moscow what it wanted, Western recognition of the post-war borders and a promise of non-intervention. But its Principle VII committed all 35 signatories to respect human rights. Dissidents seized on this. Instead of trying to reform the party, which 1968 had shown to be impossible, they demanded rights the regimes had already signed. In January 1977 **Charter 77** accused the Czechoslovak government of failing to honour those commitments. Only 243 people signed at first, and 1,621 more over ten years in a nation of 15 million; its spokesmen included the playwright Václav Havel, who urged people to "live in truth". The regime sacked, exiled and jailed signatories; in October 1979 Havel and other members of a support committee were sentenced to up to five years.

This mattered because dissidents stopped arguing with the regimes and began talking past them, which meant that Communism's own legal promises became weapons against it. Their numbers were tiny, but they offered a language of rights that others would use in 1989.

argumentsThatWork.claim: After 1968 regimes bought stability with consumer goods and asked only for outward conformity.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Romania kept stability through repression instead.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Independence from Moscow and freedom at home were different things: Romania had the first, not the second.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Romania stayed in the Warsaw Pact and Comecon, so its independence was limited.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Helsinki Accords gave dissidents a legal language of rights.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Dissident groups were tiny: Charter 77 had 243 original signatories.

howItGetsAsked: Compare and contrast the approaches of Kádár's Hungary and Ceauşescu's Romania to Soviet control between 1968 and 1980.
Examine the impact of the Helsinki Accords on opposition in eastern Europe between 1975 and 1981.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Helsinki Accords strengthened opposition in eastern Europe by giving dissidents a legal basis for their demands.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Principle VII committed all 35 signatories to respect human rights, and in January 1977 Charter 77 accused Prague of failing to honour rights it had signed.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that dissidents could demand rights the regimes already acknowledged, so they appeared moderate while forcing the regimes onto the defensive.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the movements were tiny, and the regimes could still jail them: Havel was sentenced to prison in October 1979.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Helsinki therefore changed the language of opposition more than its strength before 1980.

chunks.title: Solidarity and martial law, Poland 1976–1989
chunks.body:
Poland was different because workers and intellectuals joined forces. Food price rises had already provoked workers' revolts in 1970 and 1976. After police beat and arrested strikers at Ursus and Radom in 1976, Jacek Kuroń and others founded **KOR**, the Committee for the Defence of Workers, to give them legal help. Party leader Edward Gierek tried to buy calm by borrowing heavily abroad to subsidise food and consumer goods, but the strategy was failing.

Then came the Church. On 16 October 1978 Karol Wojtyła, Cardinal of Kraków, became **Pope John Paul II**. In June 1979 he made the first of three visits to Poland, drawing huge crowds and offering the Church not as a silent refuge but as an alternative moral authority. The regime could do nothing: banning him would only have increased his appeal.

On 1 July 1980 the government raised the price of meat. Strikes spread across the country and reached the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk on 2 August. On 14 August the electrician **Lech Wałęsa**, sacked earlier for union activity, climbed over the shipyard wall and took the lead of a national strike movement. Intellectuals such as Bronisław Geremek and Tadeusz Mazowiecki came to help the strikers negotiate. The regime gave way and conceded the right to free trade unions. On 10 November 1980 **Solidarity** became the first registered independent trade union in a Communist country, with about ten million members.

Solidarity called itself a "self-limiting revolution". Remembering 1956 and 1968, Kuroń accepted the party's "leading role", and foreign policy was kept off its agenda. But the economy was collapsing, strikes continued, and Moscow saw Poland as adrift and a bad example. General **Wojciech Jaruzelski**, prime minister from February 1981 and party leader from October, declared **martial law** on 13 December 1981, saying he was forestalling a Soviet invasion. Solidarity's leaders were imprisoned and the union was banned the next year. Martial law lasted until July 1983. When the Pope returned that June he told Jaruzelski on television that Poland must take her place "between East and West".

Judt warns against hindsight. The events of 1980–81 were the last of a series of workers' protests against economic mismanagement, not the start of Communism's fall. Michnik and Kuroń believed Communism could be eroded but not overthrown, because "power lay not in Warsaw but in Moscow". This mattered because Solidarity showed that society could organise outside the party, which meant that when Moscow's power was withdrawn after 1985, Poland already had a ready-made alternative.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Solidarity grew from the alliance of workers, intellectuals and the Church.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The immediate trigger was economic: the meat price rise of July 1980.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Its self-limitation reflected the lesson of 1956 and 1968: never challenge the party's monopoly openly.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Self-limitation did not prevent martial law.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Martial law showed that power still lay in Moscow, so Poland alone could not end Communism.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Michnik called martial law 'a disaster for the totalitarian state', since no other regime had needed it.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the rise of Solidarity in Poland between 1980 and 1981.
To what extent did the Brezhnev Doctrine secure Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1968 and 1981?

useItInAnEssay.claim: Solidarity rose so fast in 1980 because, unlike in earlier protests, workers and intellectuals acted together.
useItInAnEssay.prove: After 1976 KOR gave workers legal help, and in August 1980 intellectuals such as Geremek and Mazowiecki helped the Gdańsk strikers negotiate.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the strikers could turn a protest about meat prices into lasting demands, such as free trade unions, which the regime conceded.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the trigger was the price rise of 1 July 1980, so economic grievance still lit the fuse, as in 1970 and 1976.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The alliance of workers and intellectuals was therefore the decisive difference between 1980 and earlier Polish protests.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent did the Brezhnev Doctrine secure Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1968 and 1981?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far control rested on the Doctrine, compared with consumerism and local regimes

modelPlan.thesis: The Doctrine largely secured control by making force credible, so no regime risked reform for a decade; but it destroyed belief in reform Communism, and Poland showed that fear alone could not stop society organising.

arguments.claim: The Doctrine and the invasion made force credible (named factor first).
Normalisation and Kádárism bought conformity with consumer goods.
Romania's independence showed the Doctrine's limits.
Solidarity and martial law: control by local force.

modelPlan.counter: Control after 1968 rested as much on consumer goods and foreign loans as on the Doctrine.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did any regime abandon the party's monopoly between 1968 and 1981? None did, so the Doctrine worked, even in Poland, where the regime imposed martial law itself.

segments.text: The Brezhnev Doctrine largely secured Soviet control because it made the threat of invasion credible.
At Bratislava on 3 August 1968 Brezhnev declared that the weakening of any link affected all socialist countries, and on 21 August 500,000 Warsaw Pact troops entered Czechoslovakia.
This meant that every satellite leader knew a lapse in the party's monopoly would bring tanks, so none attempted reform for a decade.
However, in Poland ten million people joined Solidarity in 1980, which shows that fear could not stop society organising outside the party.
The Doctrine therefore secured the regimes' monopoly, but not the consent of their peoples.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The Prague Spring failed because Dubček misjudged Moscow.” Discuss with reference to 1968.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.scope: The failure of the Prague Spring
decodeKey.judgement: How far Dubček's misjudgement, rather than Moscow's fears, explains the failure

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is partly right: Dubček misread the lesson of 1956; but the deeper cause was Moscow's fear that the loss of party control would spread, which no Czech strategy short of ending reform could have removed.

arguments.claim: For: Dubček misread 1956 and reassured Moscow on the wrong point (named factor first).
For: he abolished censorship and lost control of the agenda.
Against: Moscow's fear of contagion, voiced by neighbours.
Against: the certainty that the West would not act; an invitation from five Praesidium members.

modelPlan.counter: Dubček rejected 'Two Thousand Words' and defended the monopoly, so he did not intend the outcome Moscow feared.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Could any Czech strategy short of ending reform have prevented invasion? Probably not, so Moscow's fears matter more than Dubček's judgement.

segments.text: Dubček did misjudge Moscow, but the Prague Spring failed mainly because of Soviet fears he could not remove.
The reformers believed Nagy's mistake had been leaving the Warsaw Pact, yet by 1968, as Judt argues, Moscow feared the party's loss of monopoly control more than any military threat.
This meant that Dubček's loyalty to the alliance reassured Moscow on the wrong point, while the abolition of censorship confirmed its real fear.
However, Ukrainian, Polish and East German leaders were already demanding action in March, so contagion, not Dubček's tactics, drove the decision.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: Dubček's misjudgement shaped the timing, but Moscow's fear decided the outcome.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the reasons for, and the consequences of, the rise of Solidarity in Poland between 1980 and 1981.

decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which consequence was most serious

modelPlan.thesis: Solidarity rose because workers, intellectuals and the Church acted together for the first time, with a price rise as the trigger; its main consequence was martial law, which restored control but exposed the regime's lack of legitimacy.

arguments.claim: Reason: the alliance of workers and intellectuals through KOR.
Reason: the Pope and the Church.
Consequence: free unions conceded; ten million members.
Consequence: martial law in December 1981.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues Solidarity was only the last of a series of workers' protests, so its consequences were limited until Moscow changed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted? The proof that society could organise outside the party, which outlived martial law.

segments.text: Solidarity rose so quickly in 1980 because workers and intellectuals acted together for the first time.
After 1976 KOR gave workers legal help, and in August 1980 Geremek and Mazowiecki helped the Gdańsk strikers win the right to free unions.
This meant that a protest about meat prices became a lasting organisation, registered on 10 November 1980 with about ten million members.
However, on 13 December 1981 Jaruzelski declared martial law and imprisoned its leaders, so its immediate consequences were reversed.
Solidarity's rise was therefore decisive in showing what society could do, even though martial law defeated it in 1981.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the approaches of Kádár's Hungary and Ceauşescu's Romania to Soviet control between 1968 and 1980.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The approaches of Hungary and Romania

modelPlan.thesis: Both regimes kept the party's monopoly and avoided Soviet intervention, but in opposite ways: Kádár stayed loyal to Moscow and loosened control at home, while Ceauşescu distanced Romania from Moscow and tightened control at home.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both kept the party's monopoly and avoided intervention.
Similarity: both used Western links (travel, trade) to strengthen their position.
Difference: Kádár loyal abroad, liberal at home.
Difference: Ceauşescu independent abroad, repressive at home.

modelPlan.counter: Romania's independence was limited: it stayed in the Warsaw Pact and Comecon, so the two were closer than they looked.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most to Moscow? Loyalty abroad: Moscow tolerated both because neither touched the party's monopoly or left the Pact.

segments.text: Kádár and Ceauşescu both kept their regimes safe from Moscow, but by opposite methods.

Kádár's New Economic Mechanism of 1968 allowed private plots and private shops while he reassured Moscow, whereas Ceauşescu refused Warsaw Pact manoeuvres and cut Comecon trade to 45 per cent while allowing no opposition at home.
This meant that Hungary bought domestic calm with loyalty abroad, while Romania bought independence abroad with repression at home.
However, both preserved the party's monopoly and both stayed in the Warsaw Pact, which is why Moscow tolerated both.
The decisive similarity was therefore the party's monopoly, and the decisive difference the balance between loyalty and freedom.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the impact of the Helsinki Accords on opposition in eastern Europe between 1975 and 1981.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: How far Helsinki changed opposition, compared with economic grievances and the Church

modelPlan.thesis: Helsinki changed the language and legitimacy of opposition by giving dissidents rights the regimes had signed, but the mass opposition of 1980 came from economic grievance, the Church and Polish workers.

arguments.claim: Principle VII and the Helsinki Rights movement (named factor first).
Charter 77 and the language of rights.
The regimes could still repress: Havel jailed, Ukrainian group sentenced.
In Poland mass opposition came from prices, KOR and the Church.

modelPlan.counter: The dissident movements were tiny, so Helsinki's impact on the regimes' stability was small before 1980.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did Helsinki change who opposed the regimes, or how? How: it gave a tiny opposition a legal language, while mass opposition had other causes.

segments.text: The Helsinki Accords changed how opposition in eastern Europe argued, more than how strong it was.
Principle VII committed all 35 signatories to respect human rights, and in January 1977 Charter 77 accused Prague of failing to honour rights it had signed.
This meant dissidents could appear moderate by demanding only existing legal rights, which forced the regimes onto the defensive.
However, Charter 77 had only 243 original signatories, and in October 1979 Havel was jailed, so the regimes could still contain it.
Helsinki's impact was therefore real but limited: it shaped the ideas of opposition, while mass protest grew from prices and the Church.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its reasons and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Moscow invaded mainly because the abolition of censorship threatened the party's monopoly and might spread to neighbours; an invitation from Czech hardliners and the certainty that the West would not act made the decision easy.

arguments.claim: The threat to the party's monopoly.
Fear of contagion in Ukraine, Poland and East Germany.
The Brezhnev Doctrine and the invitation from five Praesidium members.
No Western risk after the Non-proliferation Treaty.

modelPlan.counter: Brezhnev was reluctant and the decision came only on 18 August, so the invasion was not inevitable.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason would, if removed, have prevented invasion? The threat to the monopoly; without it the neighbours had nothing to fear.

segments.text: The Warsaw Pact invaded Czechoslovakia mainly because the Prague Spring threatened the party's monopoly of control.
Censorship was abolished on 26 June 1968, and the next day Vaculík called for new political parties.
This meant that the party was losing control of the agenda, which Judt argues mattered more to Moscow in 1968 than military security.
However, Brezhnev seems to have been reluctant, and fear of contagion among neighbouring leaders pushed him towards force.
The threat to the monopoly was therefore the decisive reason, with contagion turning it into an emergency.
